title: Social Contagion: the Unspoken Truth About Edu Research
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles, a self-described research enthusiast, argues that much education research published for teachers fails the test it claims to meet: measuring impact on student progress. Reviewing an issue of the Chartered College of Teaching's Impact magazine, he finds article after article offering hopeful midpoint findings, questionnaires or teacher opinion in place of learning data. He calls this a social contagion, spreading since the Visible Learning era, and sets out a seven-step pattern in which people select research that agrees with their view, implement, and never check. He is not sceptical of research but insists that without measurement an initiative is a vanity project dressed as moral purpose. He backs it with school-level Progress 8 figures and quoted passages, singling out the one piece that measured progress.
points: Salles argues that research-informed practice in schools has drifted into citing supportive studies without ever measuring the impact of the school's own implementation.
Published practitioner research often relies on questionnaires, emerging findings and opinion rather than evidence of learning progress.
He sets out a seven-step pattern of confirmation-seeking that ends in ignoring or explaining away results.
Everything works, as Hattie says, so any intervention should be measured against what the alternative would achieve.
He holds up even a tiny action-research study that measures progress as a raft of hope in a sea of wilful ignorance.
quotes: No one has noticed. No one has looked at the Emperor’s new clothes. But the approach to research in schools is not just threadbare, it is bare of any actual research.

Every article is allergic to measuring impact. They publish with hopeful findings half way through an initiative, or they rely entirely on questionnaires as measures of success. They almost always fail to measure learning.
I try to make sure everything I do in schools is data based. If we can’t put a number on it, we can’t measure it. If we don’t measure it, we’re just perpetuating our preferences.
We can justify any intervention, any change in teaching, if our only requirement is that we can quote some research which agrees with it.
This is nonsense. If we don’t measure the impact of our implementation, it is simply a vanity project dressed up as moral purpose.
And why is each finding only people’s opinions? Opinions are like underwear, nearly everybody wears one. This is not impact.
